newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends higher in Europe, unfazed by data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends higher in Europe, unfazed by data.

text.p: The dollar closed higher in European trading, taking a larger-than-expected U.S. trade gap in its stride and digesting conflicting comments from Bundesbank council members.

The U.S. unit eroded some of its morning gains on news that the country's trade deficit rose to $10.29 billion in December from a revised $7.94 billion in November. The average market expectation had been for a $9.9 billion gap but the data was within the range of forecasts.
The consumer price index rose just 0.1 percent on the month, less than the 0.3 percent increase expected.

The dollar was at 1.6943/48 marks by 1545 GMT, off a session low of 1.6806 and up from late Tuesday's European level of 1.6875/85, though still below the 34-month high of 1.7050 it hit yesterday. Against the yen it was at 124.06/16 from 123.90/95.

Neither set of data was seen as dollar-positive, with soft CPI figures taking the pressure of the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates and the trade gap growing more than expected. But analysts said the figures came as no great surprise and sentiment remained bullish.

"The U.S. data showed a largely as expected deterioration in the trade position and further evidence of the subdued nature of inflation," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at Bank of America in London. "This should tend to support the asset markets and leave the dollar little changed," he added.

U.S. Commerce Department chief economist Lee Price said faster economic growth is expected to help narrow the trade deficit this year. "While the dollar has some effects, recent history has shown that economic growth has a bigger effect on our trade balance," he told Reuters Financial Television.

The breakdown of the deficit showed a $4.27 billion shortfall with Japan, little changed from $.4.32 billion November but up 23 percent from December 1995. Overall, the U.S. trade gap reached its largest level in 1996 in seven years.
The Bundesbank's February monthly report and remarks from its chief Hans Tietmeyer weighed on the dollar in early trade here.
The report said the mark's rally since early 1995 had more than corrected, while a newspaper quoted Tietmeyer as saying he hoped the U.S. unit's rise against the mark was at an end.
But a later report quoting Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke as saying a dollar level between 1.70-1.75 marks would not risk importing inflation into Germany boosted the dollar.
Traders said a clearing bank had bought dollar/mark in size, pushing it above 1.69 and triggering stop-losses. But talk of large offers at 1.6950 capped the upside.
Confusion over the dollar's near-term direction was making trading conditions choppy.

"There's a fear it's not going to go much higher in the short term because of Bundesbank comments, but nobody's willing to short it because they feel in the medium term dollar/mark can push higher," said Chase international economist Ian Gunner.

Japan's non-seasonally-adjusted trade surplus plunged by 91.7 percent in January from a year earlier, but the Japanese Ministry of Finance (MOF) blamed the drop on seasonal factors. Analysts agreed, noting that the trade surplus was in fact 25.6 percent higher on a seasonally-adjusted basis.
Healthy buying of sterling/mark and sterling/yen also buoyed the U.S. currency, traders said.
A bigger-than-expected increase in UK January retail sales catapulted sterling higher in morning trade, helping it recoup much of Tuesday's five-pfennig loss.
The Italian lira also had a rocky ride, falling to a three-month low near 1,000 per mark in early trade before recovering to 995.70/90, up on late yesterday's 996.60/85.

It was helped by Prime Minister Romano Prodi's announcement of a mini-budget which he said would enable Italy to meet the criteria for monetary union. Fears Italy will miss the first wave of EMU have buffeted the lira in recent days.
But analysts advised caution over the budget plans, saying crucial Communist support was far from assured and questioning whether a mini-budget would have the effect Prodi promised.
-- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
